statement: As described second-hand by two narrative reviews (no primary study of this was read), tolerance to opioids is thought to fall during a period without them, so that a dose that was once usual may have a much greater effect, including on breathing, when use starts again. Neither review gives an estimate, so the evidence is insufficient to say how long a break must last, how fast tolerance falls, or by how much the chance of a fatal overdose rises. White and Irvine (1999) offer the idea as a possible explanation and rest it on one hair-analysis study (less morphine in the hair of people who died of heroin overdose than in the hair of people who were still using, which they read as a sign of lower use before death); they say that information on the rate of loss is sparse and that the loss may be quick and uneven between effects, and they describe two studies in people on methadone maintenance that found tolerance to the breathing-depressing effect of methadone to be incomplete. Hickman et al. (2008) say, citing White and Irvine, that risk appears to be raised after periods of relative abstinence, for example following incarceration or detoxification; White and Irvine write of a period of abstinence, and separately of treatment with naltrexone, and do not name either of those settings.
plain: Does tolerance drop after a break from opioids? Two review articles suggest it does: after a period without opioids, a dose that used to feel usual may have a much stronger effect, including on breathing, and that may be one reason the chance of an overdose is higher when use starts again. But the reviews give no numbers for how long a break has to be, how fast tolerance falls, or how much the risk goes up, and the main study behind the idea was one on hair samples. One review names time in prison or detox as examples; the other review it relies on does not mention them. Even people who have used opioids for a long time may keep some risk of slowed breathing, according to two studies in people on methadone. These are reviews of other people's work, not new studies, so this is an outline of what is known.
population: People who use opioids (heroin, methadone and other opioids), as described in two narrative reviews; no primary study of a break from opioids was read
exposure: A period without opioids (a period of abstinence in the reviews' wording) before use starts again
comparator: Continued regular use; the same person's tolerance before the break
outcome: Tolerance to opioid effects, including breathing depression, and the chance of a fatal overdose when use starts again
magnitude: No estimate in either source. White and Irvine (1999), second-hand: one hair-analysis study (Tagliaro et al., 1998) found lower morphine content in the hair of people who died of heroin overdose than in the hair of people who were still using (no numbers given in the review); the rate of loss of tolerance for euphoric, analgesic and respiratory effects is called sparse, probably uneven and possibly quick (receptor changes can occur in minutes or hours); incomplete tolerance to the breathing-depressing effect of methadone in two studies of people on methadone maintenance (Marks and Goldring, 1973; Santiago et al., 1977; no numbers given). Hickman et al. (2008): risk appears to be raised after periods of relative abstinence; no figures.

evidence.locator: Tolerance, paragraphs beginning 'Tolerance could also account for' and 'The loss of tolerance for the different effects'
evidence.extracted: As described by the review: tolerance could account for a relatively high risk after a period of abstinence, because loss of tolerance over time may give a much greater effect at a given dose, so that a dose that once gave euphoria with minimal breathing depression may produce pronounced respiratory impairment. It cites one study (Tagliaro and colleagues, 1998) that found less morphine in the hair of people who died of heroin overdose than in the hair of people who were still using, which it reads as suggesting a period of lower than normal use, and so lost tolerance, before death, and says that information on the rate of loss of tolerance for euphoric, analgesic and respiratory effects is sparse. It adds that the loss is likely to be non-uniform between effects and may be quite rapid, since receptor changes can take place in minutes or hours.

evidence.locator: Tolerance, paragraph beginning 'Tolerance to respiratory depression in animals'
evidence.extracted: As described by the review: tolerance to breathing depression in animals is relatively slow and incomplete compared with other opioid effects, and there is some evidence of this in people: two studies of people on methadone maintenance (Marks and Goldring, 1973; Santiago and colleagues, 1977) showed that tolerance to the breathing-depressing effect of methadone was incomplete; the review concludes that even people who have used opioids for a long time are at significant risk of breathing depression.

The review states that overdose risk appears to be increased after periods of relative abstinence, for example following incarceration or detoxification, and puts this down to lowered tolerance, citing White and Irvine; it gives no figures. White and Irvine write of a period of abstinence and of naltrexone treatment, not of incarceration or detoxification.

The review says that people who have stopped or are cutting down on heroin may drink more, and that low or falling tolerance may be the underlying problem in the link between alcohol and fatal overdose rather than a direct effect of alcohol, citing White and Irvine; lost tolerance is offered as an alternative explanation, with no data.

The review lists as an unanswered question to what extent and for how long opiate substitution drugs give tolerance to the breathing depression of heroin, that is, for how long patients are protected if they relapse or take heroin on top of a prescription.

risk_of_bias.note: The primary evidence (one hair-analysis study of people who died of overdose; two studies of people on methadone) cannot be appraised from the reviews, and the claim about breaks rests on one study that the review itself reads as suggestive.

inconsistency.note: No conflicting statement in either review.

indirectness.note: Second-hand through narrative reviews, one of which cites the other; the settings named (incarceration, detoxification) come from the later review and are not in the review it cites.

imprecision.note: No estimate is claimed; the claim states that none is available.

grade.reasoning: A claim seen only through reviews starts from the design of the primary studies they describe, here observational (a hair-analysis comparison of people who died of overdose with people who were still using) and human studies of methadone, so it starts low, and is downgraded for risk of bias (primary studies not appraisable) and for indirectness (second-hand; one review cites the other). Certainty very low. The relation is insufficient evidence because neither source gives a size, a time course or a risk figure. Because every supporting anchor is a narrative review, the claim stays at draft and says so in its statement (METHODS 6.3). Status: single study in effect (Hickman et al. rest on White and Irvine for this point). The claim keeps to what the text says: White and Irvine name only a period of abstinence, and the examples of incarceration and detoxification belong to Hickman et al.

verification.flag_note: Rests on two narrative reviews, one citing the other, so one source in effect; stays at draft. The brief's examples (prison, detox) are Hickman et al.'s addition; White and Irvine write only of a period of abstinence (their pp. 966-967) and of naltrexone treatment (p. 968), as the study cards record. The primary studies named by White and Irvine (Tagliaro et al. 1998; Marks and Goldring 1973; Santiago et al. 1977) were not read and have no reference records here; a primary study of overdose risk by time since last use, for example after release from prison or leaving a treatment programme, is the missing evidence. White and Irvine also describe, second-hand, that use in an unfamiliar setting goes with lower tolerance (Siegel 1984, p. 966), and that after two weeks of naltrexone one study found the same breathing depression from a given morphine dose (Cornish 1993, p. 968); neither is claimed here and each could become its own claim. The study cards sc_white_1999 and sc_hickman_2008 are staged in data/study-cards/_incoming/interactions/ and must be merged first.
